prompt: A standard school physics laboratory has dimensions of approximately $9\text{ m} \times 7\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$. Given that air has a density of approximately $1.2\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ at room temperature, which value is the most reasonable estimate for the mass of air contained in the room?

answer.explanation: Volume is approx 9 m x 7 m x 3 m = 189 m^3. Mass = density x volume = 1.2 kg/m^3 x 189 m^3 approx 230 kg.

distractor_explanations: Incorrect. 0.23 kg would be the mass of air in a small shoebox, not an entire laboratory.
Incorrect. 2.3 kg is the mass of air in a dustbin or small cupboard (~2 m^3).
Correct. Volume is roughly 190 m^3; multiplying by 1.2 kg/m^3 gives ~230 kg.
Incorrect. 23 000 kg (23 tonnes) is the mass of multiple fully laden transport trucks.
hints: Estimate room volume first: length x width x height.
Multiply volume by air density: m = rho x V.
solution: Room volume V approx 9 m x 7 m x 3 m = 189 m^3. Mass of air m = rho x V approx 1.2 kg/m^3 x 189 m^3 = 226.8 kg approx 230 kg. This surprising result (air in a room has mass comparable to 3 adults) is a classic physics estimation archetype. Option C is correct.
teacher_walkthrough: Classic Cambridge problem demonstrating that gases have substantial mass when aggregated over room volumes.
Show step-by-step spatial geometry multiplication followed by density scaling.
